usual_horizontal_direction: Left to right, with lines stacked top to bottom.
vertical_use: Vertical setting is not the conventional layout; when used for effect, such as on a book spine or sign, letters are usually rotated or stacked as a design choice rather than a standard script rule.
important_qualification: Historically the same letters have also been written in other directions, for example in some early inscriptions, so the modern left-to-right convention is a convention, not a property of the letters themselves.

usual_horizontal_direction: Right to left, with lines stacked top to bottom.
vertical_use: Vertical writing is not conventional for Arabic; text on tall surfaces is normally rotated as a whole line rather than written as a column.
important_qualification: Digits and embedded Latin words are still read left to right inside a right-to-left line, so a single line can contain runs in both directions (bidirectional text).

usual_horizontal_direction: Right to left, with lines stacked top to bottom.
vertical_use: Vertical layout is not a conventional Hebrew layout; columns are not used for ordinary text.
important_qualification: Numbers and quoted Latin-script words inside Hebrew text run left to right, so the visual order of a mixed line differs from its logical reading order.

usual_horizontal_direction: Left to right in most present-day general-purpose text, with lines stacked top to bottom.
vertical_use: Vertical writing is fully conventional: characters run top to bottom in columns, and columns are arranged from right to left; it remains common in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Japan and classical or literary settings.
important_qualification: The same script serves both layouts, so one book or sign may mix horizontal and vertical text; older horizontal signs were often read right to left, as one-character vertical columns.

usual_horizontal_direction: There is no usual horizontal direction; the standard layout is vertical rather than horizontal.
vertical_use: Vertical writing is the standard layout: text runs top to bottom in columns, and columns are ordered from left to right, the opposite column order to vertical Chinese.
important_qualification: When Mongolian must sit inside a horizontal line, for example in a table cell or a mixed-script document, the text is typically rotated, and the Cyrillic alphabet used for Mongolian in Mongolia is a different script written horizontally.
